title: Windows + Android
why: The card promises support for two device families. A single desktop monitor undersells Android and makes the platform coverage less obvious.
options: Shows desktop and phone together; communicates cross-platform support directly.
Useful if Android is the primary visual focus, but it downplays Windows.
Clear Windows cue, but it is not a good representation of Android support.

title: One-command installs
why: A chest reads as an in-game container. The feature is about installing software through a command or package workflow.
options: Works if the copy emphasizes downloading an installer rather than running a package command.
Suggests a package being installed or verified; less explicit about the one-command part.

title: Multiple languages
why: A quill and book suggest writing or documentation. The card describes programming-language support.
options: The angle brackets and slash read as programming, not prose.
More explicitly conveys multilingual support, though it can be mistaken for spoken languages.
Signals programming syntax and language tooling; slightly less instantly recognizable.

title: Open source
why: A gem has no clear relationship to source code, collaboration, or a public repository.
options: Communicates source control and collaborative development without tying the site to one host.
Immediately familiar to most developers, but visually associates open source with GitHub specifically.
Good for contributions and collaboration; less recognizable than a branch icon.

title: Play
why: A diamond reads as an item, reward, or currency. The role is for people who want to play the game.
options: Most direct visual for a player/gaming role.
Minecraft-like blocks reinforce the game context, but do not distinguish playing from building.
Focuses on the player rather than the game; a more human-centered option.

title: Host a server
why: A monitor describes a computer, not the server service or hosting role.
options: Rack units and status lights are a familiar server symbol.
Useful if the intended meaning is server data/storage, but hosting is broader than a database.

title: Develop
why: A pickaxe is a gameplay tool. The role takes visitors to APIs, tutorials, and mod development.
options: Simple and recognizable symbol for writing software.
Fits a developer workflow, especially command-line tools.
Suggests source files and API work; a more specific developer/document cue.

title: Mod management
why: A chest is a generic game object. For a launcher feature about mods, use a package or stack metaphor.
options: Represents installed/manageable packages, a good fit for mod management.
Suggests a stack of add-ons or layers applied to the game.
Keeps the Minecraft visual language, though it is less specific to mod management.

title: Accounts
why: A heart implies favorites or affection, not a user identity or account profile.
options: Better when the feature manages multiple player accounts.
Works when account identity/profile details are the focus; more administrative in tone.

title: About / story introduction
why: The current quill suggests writing. The first story card introduces the project and its background.
options: Good for project information and a factual overview.
A more decorative story/history cue; less neutral than an open book.

title: Why this project exists
why: A plain question mark only repeats the fact that this is a question. A concept or conversation icon gives the card more meaning.
options: Signals an idea, motivation, or reason behind the project.
Useful if the content is framed as a question-and-answer.
Keeps the question/help meaning but gives it a more deliberate visual container.

title: Contribute code / report issues
why: A pickaxe is unrelated to contributing to the software project.
options: Directly represents code contribution and review workflow.
A broad developer symbol; less explicit about contributing changes.
Suggests maintenance and fixing, but not collaboration or pull requests.

title: Donate
why: A gem suggests an item or reward. The card is explicitly about financial/community support.
options: Combines community support with a helping hand.
Simple emotional/community support cue, but less specific to donations.
Explicitly signals money; more transactional and less community-oriented.

title: Categories
why: A chest does not communicate content classification. A folder or grid is a better metaphor for grouped posts.
options: Works if categories are curated collections, but can be confused with saved posts.
Suggests a browsable collection; less clear that the items are categories.

title: About page link
why: Quotation marks imply a quote or testimonial, not an information/about page.
options: Common, compact symbol for an About or information page.
Suggests background/story content, but may overlap with documentation.
A neutral page/document cue; less specific than the information symbol.
